Breast Cancer Classification Using Logistic Regression, Neural Networks, Decision Trees, and Bagging: A Complete Comparative Analysis

Kelly Adu - Gyamfi

2025-11-20

1 Data Description

Data Source:
The Breast Cancer dataset used in this study originates from the University of Wisconsin Hospitals, Madison, Wisconsin, USA, collected by Dr. William H. Wolberg of the Department of Surgical Oncology. The dataset was designed to assist in the diagnosis of breast cancer using cytological features obtained from fine needle aspirate (FNA) samples of breast masses. Each observation corresponds to a patient’s sample, characterized by ten cytological measurements describing cell nuclei appearance, along with a diagnostic label indicating whether the tumor is benign or malignant.

Original reference:
Wolberg, W. H., & Mangasarian, O. L. (1990). Multisurface method of pattern separation for medical diagnosis applied to breast cytology. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 87(23), 9193–9196.
https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Breast+Cancer+Wisconsin+(Original)

Data Generation/Collection:
The data were collected from the University of Wisconsin Hospitals, Madison, by Dr. William H. Wolberg. Cytological measurements were taken directly from digitized images of fine needle aspirate samples. Each feature is an integer value ranging from 1 to 10, representing the degree of cell abnormality. The dataset is widely used for supervised learning and binary classification benchmarking.

Size:

  • Sample size (Number of observations): 699 total records (after cleaning: 683)

  • Variables: 11 total (10 numerical predictors, 1 categorical target)

2 Formulating Practical and Analytical Questions

Developing predictive models for breast cancer diagnosis requires translating real-world clinical needs into structured analytical questions. The goal is to use these measurable features to support early cancer detection through accurate and interpretable classification models.

2.1 Practical Questions

  1. Can cytological characteristics of breast cell nuclei reliably predict whether a tumor is benign or malignant?
  2. Which features contribute most to distinguishing malignant from benign tumors?
  3. Which modeling approach (logistic regression, neural network, decision tree, or ensemble) yields the most accurate and interpretable results?
  4. How can model predictions be optimized to minimize misclassification, especially false negatives (malignant cases predicted as benign)?
  5. Can predictive analytics assist healthcare professionals in making early and cost-effective diagnostic decisions?

2.2 Analytical Questions

  1. Can a binary classification model accurately predict tumor type (benign vs. malignant) based on cytological features?
  2. Which predictor variables show the strongest statistical or computational influence on malignancy?
  3. How do performance metrics (ROC-AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score) differ among the candidate models?
  4. Can neural network architectures (e.g., perceptrons with different activation functions) outperform classical models like logistic regression?
  5. Can decision trees and bagging ensembles improve performance by addressing nonlinearity and reducing model variance?
  6. Which optimal threshold maximizes diagnostic effectiveness while minimizing clinical misclassification costs?

4 Feature Engineering

# Feature engineering based on EDA insights
feature_engineering <- function(data) {
  engineered_data <- data %>%
    mutate(
      # Feature discretization based on clinical relevance
      Cell.size.cat = cut(Cell.size, 
                         breaks = c(0, 2, 5, 10),
                         labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
      Cl.thickness.cat = cut(Cl.thickness,
                            breaks = c(0, 3, 6, 10),
                            labels = c("Thin", "Medium", "Thick")),
      Bare.nuclei.cat = cut(Bare.nuclei,
                           breaks = c(0, 2, 5, 10),
                           labels = c("Few", "Moderate", "Many")),
      
      # Feature transformations
      Cell.size.sqrt = sqrt(Cell.size + 1),
      Cl.thickness.log = log(Cl.thickness + 1),
      
      # Feature creation: composite scores
      Nuclear.abnormality.score = (Cell.size + Cell.shape + Bare.nuclei) / 3,
      Structural.abnormality.score = (Cl.thickness + Marg.adhesion + Epith.c.size) / 3,
      
      # Risk score based on correlation insights
      High.risk.features = (Cell.size > 5) + (Cell.shape > 5) + (Bare.nuclei > 5) +
                          (Cl.thickness > 5) + (Bl.cromatin > 5)
    )
  
  return(engineered_data)
}

# Apply feature engineering
BreastCancer_engineered <- feature_engineering(BreastCancer_clean)

# Display new features
cat("New engineered features:\n")
## New engineered features:
new_features <- setdiff(names(BreastCancer_engineered), names(BreastCancer_clean))
print(new_features)

# 3. Detect abnormal patterns and outliers
detect_abnormal_patterns <- function(data) {
  # Z-score analysis for outliers
  z_scores <- scale(data[,1:9])
  outliers <- apply(z_scores, 2, function(x) sum(abs(x) > 3))
  
  # Feature ranges and variability
  feature_stats <- data.frame(
    Feature = names(data[,1:9]),
    Min = sapply(data[,1:9], min),
    Max = sapply(data[,1:9], max),
    Mean = sapply(data[,1:9], mean),
    SD = sapply(data[,1:9], sd),
    Outliers_3SD = outliers
  )
  
  return(feature_stats)
}

abnormal_patterns <- detect_abnormal_patterns(BreastCancer_clean)
kable(abnormal_patterns, caption = "Feature Statistics and Outlier Detection") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))

5 Exploratoty data analysis

5.1 Feature distributions by class

feature_distribution_analysis <- function(data) {
  data_long <- data %>%
    pivot_longer(-c(Class, Class_binary), names_to = "Feature", values_to = "Value")
  
  ggplot(data_long, aes(x = Value, fill = Class)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
    facet_wrap(~Feature, scales = "free") +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title = "Enhanced Feature Distributions by Class",
         subtitle = "Identifying class separation patterns",
         x = "Feature Value", y = "Density") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("benign" = "blue", "malignant" = "red"))
}

feature_distribution_analysis(BreastCancer_clean)

5.1.1 Summary of Key Observations from Feature Distributions

The density plots reveal clear class separation patterns between benign and malignant tumors across most cytological features.

  • Strongly Discriminatory Features: Cell.size and Cell.shape show the most distinct separation, with malignant samples concentrated at higher values (7–10) and benign ones at lower values (1–4). Bare.nuclei displays a bimodal pattern among malignant cases, suggesting variability within tumor subtypes.

  • Moderately Discriminatory Features: Cl.thickness, Marg.adhesion, Normal.nucleoli, and Bl.cromatin show partial overlap but a consistent trend of higher values for malignant cases.

  • Weakly Discriminatory Features: Epith.c.size and Mitoses have the most overlap between classes, though malignant samples still lean toward higher scores.

5.2 Correlation analysis with class relationship

correlation_analysis <- function(data) {
  # Calculate correlation with class
  cor_with_class <- sapply(data[,1:9], function(x) cor(x, data$Class_binary))
  cor_df <- data.frame(
    Feature = names(cor_with_class),
    Correlation_with_Class = round(cor_with_class, 3)
  ) %>% arrange(desc(abs(Correlation_with_Class)))
  
  # Feature correlation matrix
  cor_matrix <- cor(data[,1:9])
  
  list(
    correlation_with_class = cor_df,
    feature_correlation_matrix = cor_matrix
  )
}

5.2.1 Summary of Feature Correlation Patterns

The correlation matrix highlights key interrelationships among the nine cytological features used for breast cancer classification.

Strong Correlations (r > 0.8): Cell.size and Cell.shape show an exceptionally high positive correlation (r ≈ 0.9), indicating that abnormal cells tend to have both irregular sizes and shapes. Modeling Implication: This strong association may cause multicollinearity; dimensionality reduction or selecting only one of these variables may be necessary.

Moderate Correlations (r = 0.6–0.8): Cl.thickness shows moderate relationships with Cell.size, Cell.shape, and Marg.adhesion, suggesting these traits often change together in abnormal samples. Bare.nuclei and Normal.nucleoli also correlate moderately, reflecting coordinated nuclear changes typical of malignant cells.

Overall, the correlation structure supports known biological relationships while emphasizing the need to manage redundancy in predictive modeling

6 Feature selection using correlation and domain knowledge

feature_selection <- function(data) {
  # Calculate feature importance using random forest
  set.seed(123)
  rf_model <- train(Class ~ ., 
                   data = data %>% select(-Class_binary, -contains(".cat")),
                   method = "rf",
                   trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5))
  
  # Get variable importance
  var_imp <- varImp(rf_model)$importance
  var_imp$Feature <- rownames(var_imp)
  var_imp <- var_imp %>% arrange(desc(Overall))
  
  return(var_imp)
}

# Select top features
selected_features <- feature_selection(BreastCancer_engineered)
top_features <- head(selected_features$Feature, 8)  # Select top 8 features

cat("Top selected features:\n")

7.2 Final Logistic Regression Equation

The estimated logistic regression model predicting the probability of a tumor being malignant is given by:

\[ \text{logit}\!\left[P(\text{malignant})\right] = -23.4517 + 0.7919(\text{Nuclear.abnormality.score}) + 1.2167(\text{Structural.abnormality.score}) + 0.3969(\text{High.risk.features}) + 0.0227(\text{Cell.shape}) + 11.9366(\text{Cell.size.sqrt}) - 2.7230(\text{Cell.size}) - 0.0085(\text{Epith.c.size}) \]

where

\[ \text{logit}(p) = \log\!\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) \]

and therefore,

\[ P(\text{malignant}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\text{logit}(p)}} \]

Interpretation of Coefficients:

  • A one-unit increase in Structural.abnormality.score multiplies the odds of malignancy by \(e^{1.2167} \approx 3.38\), holding other variables constant.
  • A one-unit increase in Nuclear.abnormality.score multiplies the odds by \(e^{0.7919} \approx 2.21\).
  • Cell.size.sqrt has a strong positive association (\(\beta = 11.9366\)), while Cell.size has a strong negative association (\(\beta = -2.7230\)), indicating a nonlinear effect of cell size on malignancy probability.
  • The coefficient for Epith.c.size is near zero, suggesting minimal contribution to the model.
  • Bare.nuclei was excluded (missing coefficients) due to perfect or quasi-perfect separation, a common issue in cytological datasets.

9.1 Summary

Key Observations - The Perceptron model with tanh activation achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.9932), indicating the strongest overall discriminative ability among all models.
- The Regularized Logistic Regression also performed exceptionally well (ROC-AUC = 0.9923), with slightly higher sensitivity (0.9775) than the perceptrons—important for detecting malignant cases.
- All models maintained accuracy around 94–95%, confirming consistent predictive reliability across different algorithms.
- The Perceptron models demonstrated superior specificity (0.9583) and precision (≈0.977), showing strong performance in correctly classifying benign samples and minimizing false positives.

Conclusion: Both Regularized Logistic Regression and the Perceptron (tanh) model exhibited near-perfect classification performance on the validation data.
While the logistic model offers interpretability and clinical transparency, the perceptron provides slightly higher ROC-AUC and balanced error rates, suggesting its potential as a high-performing nonlinear alternative for automated cancer classification tasks.

Both models exhibit exceptionally strong classification ability, as indicated by their near-perfect curvature toward the top-left corner of the plot, where sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (1 − false positive rate) are maximized.

10.1.1 Key Observations

  • The Logistic Regression model achieved an AUC of 0.9923, while the Perceptron model achieved an AUC of 0.9913.
  • These values are almost identical, confirming that both algorithms perform at an expert diagnostic level in distinguishing malignant from benign breast tumors.
  • The overlapping curves suggest that both models maintain high sensitivity and specificity, with minimal trade-off between correctly identifying malignant samples and avoiding false positives.
  • The slight edge of the logistic model (AUC = 0.9923) reflects its stable linear decision boundary, whereas the perceptron’s comparable AUC demonstrates the power of even simple nonlinear transformations for this dataset.

10.2 Conclusion

Both models demonstrate excellent diagnostic accuracy, with AUC values > 0.99, which far exceed the typical clinical benchmark for strong classifiers (AUC > 0.90).
These findings suggest that the models could effectively serve as part of a decision-support system for early cancer detection, balancing sensitivity and specificity to minimize diagnostic errors.

12 Decision Tree Model

# Decision Tree model development
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)

# Train decision tree with different complexity parameters
set.seed(123)
tree_model <- train(Class ~ .,
                    data = train_data,
                    method = "rpart",
                    trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5),
                    tuneGrid = expand.grid(cp = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1)))

# Display optimal complexity parameter
cat("Optimal Complexity Parameter (cp):", tree_model$bestTune$cp, "\n")
## Optimal Complexity Parameter (cp): 0.1
# Make predictions
tree_pred <- predict(tree_model, newdata = test_data)
tree_prob <- predict(tree_model, newdata = test_data, type = "prob")[,2]
tree_cm <- confusionMatrix(tree_pred, test_data$Class)
# Plot the decision tree
rpart.plot(tree_model$finalModel, 
           main = "Decision Tree for Breast Cancer Classification",
           box.palette = "Blues",
           shadow.col = "gray",
           nn = TRUE)

12.1 Decision Tree Summary

Primary Splitting Feature: The tree uses Bare.nuclei as the root node, indicating it’s the most important predictor for classifying breast tumors as benign or malignant.

12.1.1 Key Decision Rules:

  • Low-risk path: Samples with Bare.nuclei < 3 are predominantly benign (92% benign probability)

  • High-risk path: Samples with Bare.nuclei ≥ 3 require further examination of Cell.size

– If Cell.size < 4: Mostly benign (96% benign probability)

– If Cell.size ≥ 4: Mostly malignant (90-95% malignant probability)

12.1.2 Performance Insights:

  • The tree shows clear separation with some terminal nodes reaching 95% malignant probability

  • Cell.size serves as the critical secondary feature for cases with ambiguous Bare.nuclei values

  • Multiple terminal nodes achieve very high purity (0.00-0.01 benign probability in some malignant nodes)

12.1.3 Clinical Utility:

This tree provides a simple, interpretable decision pathway that could be easily implemented in clinical settings, using just two key cytological features to achieve high classification accuracy.

13 Bagging Algorithm

Bagging, short for Bootstrap Aggregating, is an ensemble learning technique used to reduce model variance and improve prediction stability. Instead of relying on a single decision tree, bagging creates many bootstrap samples of the training data and trains a separate tree on each one. The final prediction is obtained by averaging probabilities or taking a majority vote across all trees.

This approach helps overcome the biggest weakness of decision trees: high sensitivity to small changes in the training data, which can cause instability. By combining many trees, bagging produces a more robust and more accurate classifier.

bagging_test_metrics <- calculate_metrics(
  actual        = test_data$Class,
  predicted     = bagging_pred,
  probabilities = bagging_prob,
  model_name    = "Bagging_Test"

14 Overall Summary of Model Performance

Four models were evaluated on the test set: Logistic Regression, Perceptron Neural Network, Decision Tree, and Bagging Ensemble. Their performance was compared using key diagnostic metrics including ROC-AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score.

The results reveal clear differences in classification strength:

14.1 Logistic Regression

  • Strong ROC-AUC (0.9932), indicating good discriminative ability

  • However, test accuracy was only 65%, with specificity dropping to 0

  • This means the model failed to correctly identify malignant samples

  • Best suited when interpretability is needed, not optimal for this dataset’s nonlinear patterns

14.2 Perceptron Neural Network

  • Excellent ROC-AUC (0.9949) and high accuracy (0.9704)

  • Very balanced performance across sensitivity and specificity

  • Captures nonlinear relationships better than logistic regression

  • A strong candidate, but not the top performer

14.3 Decision Tree

  • Achieved perfect performance across all metrics:

  • ROC-AUC = 1.0000

  • Accuracy = 1.0000

  • Sensitivity = 1.0000

  • Specificity = 1.0000

  • Precision = 1.0000

  • F1 = 1.0000

  • The tree fully separated malignant from benign cases

  • Provides interpretability through simple, rule-based splits

  • This was the highlighted top performer in your table

14.4 Bagging Ensemble

  • Also achieved perfect scores on every metric

  • Bagging stabilizes predictions by averaging many bootstrapped trees

  • Reduced variance, stronger generalization, and perfect class separation

  • Slightly more robust than a single tree due to the ensemble structure

14.5 ROC Curve Summary

14.5.1 The ROC analysis reinforced the tabular results:

  • Logistic regression and perceptron showed strong curves bending sharply toward the top left corner, reflecting excellent discrimination.

  • Decision Tree and Bagging both produced AUC = 1.000, indicating perfect ranking ability with no overlap between malignant and benign distributions.

  • The Bagging model’s ROC curve was identical to the Decision Tree curve, confirming flawless classification.

14.6 Best Overall Model

14.6.1 Bagging Ensemble (Best Model)

Although both the Decision Tree and Bagging Ensemble achieved perfect scores, Bagging is the best overall model because:

  • It reduces the instability of single trees

  • It maintains perfect performance while providing stronger robustness

  • It generalizes better on datasets prone to noise

  • It represents a superior ensemble-based learning approach

Therefore, based on ROC-AUC and all test metrics, the Bagging Ensemble is selected as the best-performing classifier for this breast cancer dataset.
